extracted.intended_audience: literate English readers / subscribers of The Spectator (early-18th-century general readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral, social and satirical periodical essays (Spectator-style) that offer prescriptive reflections on manners, fashion, honour, and conversation for a general reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive female head-dress (Fontange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not load the head with 'a Pile of supernumerary Ornaments' that 'destroy the Symmetry of the human Figure' and call off the eye 'from great and real Beauties, to childish Gewgaws, Ribbands, and Bone-lace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: fourteenth-century 'Fontanges' rose an ell above the head, pointed like steeples, with long crape streamers. Anti-patterns: fashions so extreme women appear as 'Colossus' with head-dress; mobs burned or pelted these ornaments. Prescription: recommend prevention — consider it impossible to add ornament to the masterpiece of Nature; appeal to symmetry and natural beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: When judging older writers, make allowances for obsolete words and allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret remote hints and obsolete phrases with indulgence; assume many oddities aim at contemporary follies now obscure to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spectator's seeming improbabilities (puppet-shows, patches as attestations, chairs as actors) should be read as allusions to then-current follies. Critical readers should allow for 'the Mirth and Humour of the Author' and not apply literal modern standards to remote references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of Honour: men—courage; women—chastity
rubrics_metrics.description: The great Point of Honour in Men is Courage, and in Women Chastity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: each sex values the qualification that renders them most amiable to the other. Alternative ideals (men choosing wisdom/virtue; women choosing wit/good-nature) are suggested but the prevailing point remains. Examples from chivalry and Spain illustrate extreme fixation on these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving the lie is the chief violation of honour among men
rubrics_metrics.description: The great Violation of the Point of Honour from Man to Man is giving the Lie; to say a man Lies is an affront that 'nothing but Blood can expiate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: calling someone a liar implies cowardice. Cultural practice: training in truthfulness considered as important as horsemanship and archery for Persians. Anti-pattern: using 'lie' as a casual insult invites duels and violent reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: False notions of honour (duelling) should be discouraged and punished
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'refuse of Mankind' set up for Men of Honour by a false sense of courage; such practices (duelling) are absurd and should be reduced by shameful punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested remedy: public shame (e.g., pillory) in addition to or instead of death to reduce duelling; note the practical effect of making duelling both dangerous and dishonourable to discourage it. When honour contradicts religion and equity it becomes a 'Depravation of human Nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Honour must align with religion, equity, and virtuous principles
rubrics_metrics.description: When Honour is a Support to virtuous Principles... it cannot be too much cherished; but when the Dictates of Honour are contrary to those of Religion and Equity, they are the greatest Depravations of human Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate honourable actions by whether they run parallel with laws of God and country; governments should 'explode' such honour-codes that promote wrong ambitions and false ideas of laudable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a disposition to be pleased—mutual good humour in company
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain a disposition to be pleased and place oneself in a constant aptitude for the satisfactions of being; mutual good humour is a 'Dress we ought to appear in whenever we meet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: affected delicacy, valetudinarians who relate aches/pains in company, indolence that reduces life to mere vegetative existence. Positive examples: Varilas, whose 'portable Quality of good Humour' seasons conversation; being pleasant requires avoiding shocking or self-centered topics and contributing to others' pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation should present excellence and avoid shocking or degrading content
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful Pictures are the Entertainments of pure Minds; enjoy conversation 'wherein there is nothing presented but in its Excellence'—this is a degree towards the life of angels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: companies where speakers represent others without ill-will and set things in the best light offer delicate entertainment. Anti-patterns: conversation that dwells on deformities or shocks; people who 'set it in the best light' produce superior social pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity in conversation; avoid hollow compliments and dissimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'great and general Want of Sincerity in Conversation.' Compliment and dissimulation make words 'hardly any signification of their thoughts'—words become 'mere Cyphers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: the best way to seem a quality is to have it; pretence is as troublesome as possession and is often discovered. Long-term harm: dissimulation brings 'everlasting Jealousie and Suspicion' so that a man is not believed when he speaks truth. Prescription: prefer plainness, honesty, and avoid the inflated currency of empty compliments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure and fame: eminence invites censure; posterity balances reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Censure 'is the Tax a Man pays to the Publick for being Eminent.' Eminent persons cannot escape reproach; posterity has the privilege to adjust characters impartially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectation for public figures: accept censure as concomitant to greatness; later historians (less partisan) will give a balanced account. This is a principle for assessing contemporary reputations and anticipating re-evaluation over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Exercise of the Fan: a codified social skill with named maneuvers and timings
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'Academy for the training up of young Women in the Exercise of the Fan' uses commands: 'Handle your Fans, Unfurl your fans, Discharge your Fans, Ground your Fans, Recover your Fans, Flutter your Fans.' Mastery is progressive and expresses emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed guidance: 'handle' learned in a week (close fan shakes, taps, gestures); 'unfurl' requires about a month's practice (flirts, vibrations, revealing pictures); 'discharge' (a loud crack) is difficult—can be trained to make a pop like a pocket-pistol; 'ground' may be learned in two days (tossing aside gracefully); 'recover' requires attention; 'flutter' (master-piece) about three months and includes varieties: angry, modest, timorous, confused, merry, amorous. Fans serve as social signalling: type of flutter reveals emotion; fans can be engineered (e.g., devices to amplify crack). Anti-patterns: misusing fan cracks at unsuitable times; mishandling reduces social grace.
